newsitem.title: POLAND: POLISH YIELDS SEEN DOWN ON TIGHTER BUDGET PLEDGE.
newsitem.headline: POLISH YIELDS SEEN DOWN ON TIGHTER BUDGET PLEDGE.

text.p: Polish yields are likely to drop in the longer term if Finance Minister Marek Belka's Wednesday statements signalling that a lower budget deficit could be in store in 1998 come true, analysts said.

Analysts said that a lower budget gap next year would shift part of the burden of keeping the Polish economy's growth in check from restrictive monetary policy of the central bank toward a tighter fiscal policy by the government.

"Yields will fall in the longer term as the tighter fiscal policy cools Poland's economic climate without forcing further interest rate increases," said Rafal Petsch, dealer at Bank of America in London.

Belka said the 1997 budget gap target would not be surpassed, but said that next year's budget defict would be difficult to finance if it remained unchanged at 2.8 percent of the gross domestic product (GDP).
He said also that the finance ministry was having trouble placing paper on markets, which analysts said referred to the situtation on the local T-bill market earlier in the year.
In the first four months of 1997, T-bill yields grew more than two percentage points to nearly 22 percent in low demand before the trend reverse over the last month.
Belka said that next year's budget deficit would probably be higher than the 1.8 percent of GDP figure given by the central bank president on Tuesday.
"I don't know whether the budget deficit will be on the scale as the central bank president said, but we are certanily going in that direction," Belka told a news conference.

Analysts took Belka's statements with a grain of salt, saying that a large reduction in the budget deficit would mean increasing taxes or slashing spending, which may prove to be difficult following this September's parliamentary polls.
"There is still a long way to go for this plan to become law and implementing such a tight budget could be difficult," said Wojciech Kowalczyk, senior dealer at Bank Handlowy SA.
Analysts said that curbing the deficit would likely envision a shift in financing the budget deficit from shorter-term Treasury bills to longer T-bonds.

"Poland must use longer financial instruments in order to cut the costs of its budget deficit, but in order to make T-bonds attractive to investors a liquid secondary market must first be created," Handlowy's Kowalczyk said.
